**`POS-035` — Unified audit log ingestion.** Attack simulation reporting depends on this, and the Simulations tab says so in a banner that names a quarter of the reason. The full chain is five links and no course guide mentions any of it: simulation reporting needs unified audit logging, which needs a hydrated Exchange organisation (POS-036), which new/trial tenants do not have, and which propagates unevenly across Exchange backend servers. Discovered because the banner appeared, not because anything failed. The campaign launched cleanly, status In progress, no errors anywhere. Had the banner been dismissed the report would have been empty and the lab would have concluded that attack simulation does not report. The portal could not do this. System > Audit rendered TWO independent faults at once - "Sorry, we're having trouble figuring out if activity is being recorded" and "Failed to load data" - and offered a "Start recording user and admin activity" button. That button renders both when auditing is genuinely off AND when the page cannot determine state, so it is not evidence either way. Clicking it produced a "Complete organizational setup" prompt, accepting that produced a Client Error, and the page then unlocked its form and removed the button while STILL being unable to report state. UI advanced, operation did not. Resolved by cmdlet, which answered instantly what the page could not answer at all: Get-AdminAuditLogConfig returned False. The state was always readable; only the page could not read it. Prior state therefore measured, not assumed - the failed portal attempt changed nothing. ENDPOINT TRAP. Get-AdminAuditLogConfig also exists in Security & Compliance PowerShell, where UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled reads False even when auditing is ON (Microsoft Learn, audit-log-enable-disable). Run in the wrong endpoint it returns a permanently false value with nothing to distinguish it from a true one. This is the same shape as POS-034's corrected finding (two stores behind one query language) and the Lab 04 surface distinction - a third instance, now in PowerShell rather than KQL. Same command, different service endpoint, different meaning. Vendor claim vs measurement: the cmdlet warns "could take up to 60 minutes to take effect" and Microsoft Learn separately states audit events may take several hours to become searchable. Those are two different delays and only the first gates event capture. The property read back False immediately after a successful Set and True on a later read. Why it was off is not established. One secondary source states trial tenants are not auto-enabled for audit logging unlike new enterprise tenants, which fits this tenant exactly, but that is a blog claim rather than Learn and is recorded as a candidate explanation only. Cost: none. Audit data lives in the Microsoft 365 substrate, not in law-lab- 01. The billable surface measured on 2026-07-26 (POS-034) is unchanged. It becomes an ingestion cost only if the Office 365 connector is later added to Sentinel, which is a separate decision.

**`POS-036` — Exchange organisation customization (tenant hydration).** New Microsoft 365 tenants are provisioned dehydrated - they share an out-of- the-box configuration for objects like role assignment and mailbox policies instead of receiving unique copies. Before any of that can be altered, Enable-OrganizationCustomization must move the tenant to a customizable state. It runs explicitly, or implicitly when an admin changes a standard setting for the first time. It is a one-time operation with no way to reset IsDehydrated. Recorded as a posture entry because it is an IRREVERSIBLE tenant-level state change and because it is invisible: nothing in the portal surfaces hydration state, and the tenant had already crossed it before this lab read the value. In a tenant expiring 2026-08-13 the irreversibility costs nothing, which is why it was accepted without hesitation - that is a judgement about this environment, not a general one. (Expiry moved to 2026-09-14 on 2026-08-06, POS-077. Thirty-two more days does not make an irreversible change reversible; the judgement is unchanged.) THE FINDING - a property read is not a capability test. Within one PowerShell session, three tests disagreed. Get-OrganizationConfig returned IsDehydrated False. Enable-OrganizationCustomization returned "not required, organization is already enabled for customization." And Set- AdminAuditLogConfig failed with InvalidOperationInDehydratedContextException, naming target AdminAuditLogConfig. Two sources said hydrated; the one operation that actually attempted work said otherwise. Resolved by waiting. Roughly thirty minutes later the identical Set executed and returned only its warning. So the org-level flag was true while a specific consolidated object beneath it had not yet been instantiated - per- object propagation behind an org-level boolean. Measured window: the object rejected the write at 00:23:43 GMT and accepted it within the next ~30 minutes. Microsoft documents org hydration and says nothing about propagation behind it; this number does not exist in the vendor documentation. The three exception timestamps also crossed a different backend server than the successful reads, which is consistent with distributed propagation but was not isolated and is not claimed as the cause. Generalises past Exchange: an org-level status property answered "yes" for a capability that was not yet usable. That is POS-011's shape - configured is not effective - reached from a property rather than a portal label.

**`POS-037` — Attack simulation campaign - My First Attack Simulation Training.** The first Defender for Office 365 capability in this lab and the first that tests people rather than machines. MDO Plan 2 rides on the E5 trial; no Azure resource, no VM, no ingestion cost. Scoping decision: all-users targeting plus an explicit exclusion of the admin, rather than selecting labuser directly. One extra click, two mechanics tested instead of one - whether all-users resolves correctly, and whether the exclusion list actually excludes. Both held: every denominator in the report reads /1. MEASURED RESULTS. Delivery ~1 minute after launch, to the Focused Inbox, bypassing tenant filtering entirely. First link clicked 2h55m11s and first credential entered 2h58m37s after launch (both operator-driven, so they measure nothing about the platform except that it recorded them). Training assignment notifications arrived ~90 seconds behind each trigger. Actual compromise rate 100%, predicted 37%, users who reported 0%. Two training modules were assigned, not one: "Business Email Compromise | ClickedPayload" and "Ransomware | Compromised". The recommendation engine assigns per BEHAVIOUR exhibited, not per user - confirmed three independent ways (two named modules in the report, two notification emails three minutes apart, two distinct assignmentId GUIDs in EmailUrlInfo). THE DETECTION FINDING - and it goes further than expected. Zero incidents and zero alerts over a one-week window, which was predicted: Microsoft exempts its own simulations, because a 5,000-user drill that raised 5,000 incidents would bury the SOC that scheduled it. But the payload is also absent from EmailEvents and EmailUrlInfo entirely, while the training notifications either side of it are recorded normally in both. The tables were working; the payload is not in them. So attack simulation training tests USERS. It cannot validate detection, because it is engineered not to trigger it, and it cannot be hunted, because it leaves no telemetry to hunt. Two symmetrical misreadings follow: seeing no alert and concluding phishing detection is broken (it was told to stand down), or seeing no alert and concluding the tenant is covered (nothing about detection was exercised). Neither the course guide nor the portal says this anywhere. Two sending infrastructures, deliberately split. The drill came from templatern.com and landed the victim on sharepointle.com - a lookalike of sharepointonline.com, attacker-shaped and untelemetered. The notifications come from attacksimulationtraining.com, plainly labelled and recorded as ordinary mail. The typosquat is correct design: the address bar is where a trained user actually catches a credential harvest, so making it obviously Microsoft would invalidate the exercise. It also means allow-listing for simulations spans more than the sender domain - a tenant with strict DNS or egress filtering could deliver the mail and break the click, which would read as a user who did not engage rather than a control that intervened. Exemption is not total. Outlook still blocked remote content because the sender was not in Safe Senders. The simulation is exempt from FILTERING but not from client-side rendering protections - two mechanisms the guide's "harmless messages get through" framing collapses into one. What this campaign cannot show, foreclosed by the 2026-08-13 tenant expiry and by n=1: trend across campaigns, repeat-offender behaviour (needs consecutive compromises), and training-threshold reassignment at 90 days. Recorded as foreclosed rather than untested. A 100% compromise rate with one target is arithmetic, not a measurement. FORECLOSURE PARTIALLY LIFTED 2026-08-06 (POS-077). The expiry moved to 2026-09-14, so trend-across-campaigns and repeat-offender behaviour are no longer foreclosed by the clock - they are now merely UNTESTED, which is a different status and the register distinguishes them deliberately. The 90-day training-threshold reassignment stays foreclosed: 90 days from the 2026-07-27 campaign lands well past 2026-09-14, and the extension is spent. The n=1 limitation is unaffected by any date.

**`POS-038` — End-user notification delivery preferences (simulation-scoped).** Inherited, not decided - recorded because documentation-standard.md section 2 treats a silently inherited default as a finding when it is labelled as one. The consequence is asymmetric and works against the feature's purpose. A user who falls for the phish gets a landing page, two training modules, and weekly reminders. A user who correctly REPORTS it gets nothing at all, because positive reinforcement ships pre-set to Do not deliver. The behaviour the whole capability exists to encourage is the only one with no feedback path. Confirmed from the data rather than the wizard: the report shows "Positive Reinforcement Message Delivered 0/0". The denominator is zero, not one - the metric knows the notification was never in play, rather than recording a delivery that failed. Cleanest possible evidence for an inherited default. Not observed: the tenant-wide Settings tab (repeat offender threshold, training threshold). Those were never opened, so they are absent from this register rather than recorded from the guide's stated values.

**`POS-039` — Phish landing page - payload indicators.** Observed on the landing page after compromise: the "Tips to identify the phishing message" panel was collapsed and empty, and the reproduced email below it carried no annotations - nothing marking the urgency language, the mismatched sender, the fake deletion deadline, or the lookalike domain. So the educational moment is a verbatim copy of the message that just fooled the user, with nothing pointing at why. The user is shown the evidence and left to infer the lesson. Enabling payload indicators is one checkbox in the same wizard step. An inherited default that measurably weakens the training value of the whole exercise, on the one screen the compromised user is guaranteed to read. Also observed: the template renders a broken companyLogo placeholder when no logo is uploaded, rather than degrading gracefully. Cosmetic, but it is the default experience.

**`POS-040` — User reported settings (Outlook/Teams report button routing and feedback).** Read-only visit to Defender > Settings > Email & collaboration > User reported settings during module 53. Nothing was saved and no Save exists for what was done. The page was opened, read, and left. Assigned to lab 09 because these settings govern the "users who reported 0%" metric that lab measured, and because Microsoft's SecOps-mailbox guidance for this setting is specifically about Attack simulation training. OBSERVATION CREATED STATE. Get-ReportSubmissionPolicy returned DefaultReportSubmissionPolicy with WhenCreatedUTC = 2026-07-27 12:56:04, WhenChangedUTC identical. The tenant was created 2026-07-14, so this object did not ship with it - it was instantiated thirteen days later, roughly 44 minutes after that morning's CI push, inside the window in which this page was first opened. Written once, never modified. A secondary source states that visiting the page for the first time creates the default report submission policy; this is the direct measurement of that claim. Microsoft Learn documents the resulting default state and does not mention that reading the page produces it. The consequence is uncomfortable and worth stating plainly: reading configuration can write configuration, so an audit is not necessarily a non-event. BLANK IS NOT UNSET, AND THE DESTINATION IS IN NEITHER OBJECT. The portal shows "Send reported items to: Microsoft and my reporting mailbox" with the mailbox field empty - confirmed placeholder, not a saved value, by the Suggested contacts autocomplete appearing on click. Per Microsoft Learn this blank field IS the documented default, and it means the reporting mailbox is the global admin's Exchange Online mailbox, which is not displayed on the page until after the first user in the organisation reports a message from Outlook. The cmdlets agree and sharpen it: the policy carries ReportJunkToCustomizedAddress True and ReportPhishToCustomizedAddress True - send to a customised address - while Get-ReportSubmissionRule, the object that would define that address, returns nothing at all. Configuration split across two objects, one absent, and the operative value present in neither. The only way to learn where reports go is to send one. POS-011's shape at a third polarity. POS-011 is a healthy status over a dead control. POS-036 is an error over an operation that succeeded. This is a BLANK FIELD OVER A LIVE DESTINATION - reports have a real recipient and no surface will tell you which until the control is exercised. FOUR DEFAULTS, ALL SILENT ON SUCCESS. Ask the user to confirm before reporting: off. Show a success message after the message is reported: off. Automatically email users the results of the investigation: off. Positive reinforcement notification (POS-038): Do not deliver. A user who correctly reports a phish receives no prompt, no confirmation, no result, and no reinforcement - four independent inherited defaults across two feature areas, all pointing the same way. A user who FAILS gets a landing page, two training modules, and weekly reminders. The tenant is configured, by inheritance rather than decision, to give zero feedback for the behaviour the capability exists to encourage. This does not explain lab 09's 0% reported - labuser simply did not report - but it explains why no one would learn that reporting is worth doing. SECOPS MAILBOX GAP, UNRESOLVED. Microsoft Learn instructs that the reporting mailbox be identified as a SecOps mailbox in the advanced delivery policy, and states this is especially important when Attack simulation training is in use, because otherwise a user-reported message might trigger a training assignment by the simulation product. This tenant's reporting mailbox is the global admin's by default and is NOT configured as a SecOps mailbox, while the lab 09 campaign ran live until 2026-07-28 16:20. The interaction was not tested and reporting the simulation would have falsified lab 09's committed 0% figure. Recorded as a known unexercised interaction rather than a demonstrated one. Confirmed and requiring no action: built-in Outlook Report button selected over a non-Microsoft add-in (EnableThirdPartyAddress False), Monitor reported messages in Outlook on, Monitor reported items in Microsoft Teams on, reporting from quarantine allowed, EnableReportToMicrosoft True. Submissions baseline clean on 2026-07-27 - Emails 0 pending / 0 completed and User reported 0 across all four categories over a 7-day window, so any future report has an unambiguous before-state. The User reported tab classifies reports into four categories - Threats, Spam, No threats, and SIMULATIONS. Microsoft treats a user's report of its own drill as a distinct type rather than folding it into Threats. Set against lab 09's finding that the simulation payload leaves no EmailEvents or EmailUrlInfo row, the asymmetry is notable: the message is invisible to hunting, but a user's report of it has a dedicated counter waiting. Timestamp trap, eighth occurrence, and the first with a labelled companion property sitting beside the ambiguous one. WhenCreated read 5:56:04 AM and WhenCreatedUTC read 12:56:04 PM - exactly seven hours, the same offset measured across the two portal exports on 2026-07-26. Every prior occurrence required inferring the offset from context; Exchange objects carry both forms and name one of them. Read the *UTC properties.

| ID | Setting | Location | State | Kind | Revisit | Verified |

| `POS-043` | Microsoft 365 alert policy - LAB-BEC-Forwarding-Rule-Created | `Defender portal > Email & collaboration > Policies & rules > Alert policy` | Custom policy, Medium, Threat management, activity MailRedirect, no conditions, All users, every-time trigger, admin recipient, no daily notification limit, enabled 2026-07-28 19:09 | hardened | yes | 2026-07-28 |

**`POS-043` — Microsoft 365 alert policy - LAB-BEC-Forwarding-Rule-Created.** Created 2026-07-28 19:09 local (UTC-07:00) at Email & collaboration > Policies & rules > Alert policy. Name LAB-BEC-Forwarding-Rule-Created, Medium, category Threat management, activity MailRedirect, no conditions, scope All users, trigger "every time an activity matches", recipient the admin only, enabled on creation. The first detection AUTHORED in this environment rather than supplied by Microsoft - see DET-003 and Lab 10. LICENSING CONFIRMED BY OBSERVATION. All three trigger types rendered: every- time, threshold, and unusual volume. The latter two require E5 or a Defender for Office 365 P2 / M365 E5 Compliance / eDiscovery add-on, so their presence is a live entitlement check rather than an inference from the SKU. INHERITED DEFAULT 1 - the threshold trigger is PRE-SELECTED, at 15 activities in 60 minutes. In a three-identity tenant no threshold policy on any activity would ever fire. Accepting the default would produce a policy that is enabled, correctly configured, and structurally silent - and the guidance about that failure mode sits three sections away from the page that pre-selects it. Changed deliberately to every-time. INHERITED DEFAULT 2 - the daily notification limit defaults to NO LIMIT. An unconditioned, all-user, every-time policy is therefore an unmetered mail generator by default. Left uncapped here because a cap could suppress the notification being measured; that is a test decision, not an endorsement. Eighth inherited silent-or-noisy default recorded in this register. FRIENDLY LABEL VS SCHEMA VALUE. The picker offers "Created mail forward/redirect rule"; the stored condition reads "Activity is MailRedirect", and MailRedirect is the string that appears in the alert body and in the unified audit log. The label is UI sugar over the schema value, and the schema value is the one you hunt on. Nothing in the wizard says so - it surfaces only on the review page. THE POLICY WAS REDUNDANT AND NOBODY CHECKED. A built-in policy, "Creation of forwarding/redirect rule", covers the same activity and fired alongside this one at Informational - same activity, same user, same timestamp, two alerts, two emails, identical Details text. This tenant holds 49 alert policies, 48 of them built-in. The design step that was missed is trivial: search the existing policies before authoring a new one. Its absence produced duplicate alerting on the very first custom policy in the tenant, which is how alert fatigue actually starts - not from bad policies but from unexamined overlap with the ones already present. The duplication stops at the mailbox. Correlation produced ONE incident (ID 2), and it took this policy's name and Medium severity rather than the built-in's Informational. So the cost is notification noise, not queue noise. SEVERITY IS THE ONLY FIELD THIS POLICY CHANGED. Both emails carry identical Details text, so that string is a property of the ACTIVITY, not of the policy. The description written here - carrying the MITRE T1114.003 reference - appears in no notification and exists only in the portal. FIRST WORKING SECURITY NOTIFICATION PATH IN THIS TENANT. POS-042 records Defender XDR with no notification rules at all across incidents, actions and threat analytics, and the real incident Lab 03 produced on 2026-07-18 told nobody. Alert policies are a separate Purview-side mechanism, so this does not contradict POS-042 - it sharpens it. The capability exists in this tenant; it does not exist where the incident queue lives. Measured end to end, 2026-07-28: policy enabled 19:09, inbox rule saved 19:14, activity recorded 02:15:00 UTC (19:15 local), both emails delivered 19:18. Roughly four minutes from action to notification. The source guidance says only "give it time"; this is the number. Dependency worth stating: this detects nothing without unified audit logging (POS-035), which was off until 2026-07-27 and was enabled during Lab 09 for an unrelated reason. Had that not happened, this policy would have been created, enabled, and silent. Production answer: check the built-in policies before authoring a custom one, scope by user or condition rather than All users, set a daily notification limit, and send to a monitored SecOps mailbox rather than an individual admin. Left in the lab-shaped configuration deliberately so the trigger would be unambiguous.

Medium, T1110. Tuned - frequency 1 day to 1 hour. Has never fired. | hardened | yes | 2026-07-30 |
| `POS-046` | Sentinel analytics rule - LAB-Bruteforce-Failed-Signins (authored) | `Defender portal > Microsoft Sentinel > Configuration > Analytics > Active rules` | Authored 2026-07-30 20:00. Scheduled, Low, T1110, 5 min frequency over 1 h lookback, suppression 1 h added 2026-07-31 after measuring 12 alerts from one event. | hardened | yes | 2026-07-31 |

**`POS-045` — Sentinel analytics rule - Brute force attack against Azure Portal (Microsoft template, tuned).** Microsoft's Content Hub template "Brute force attack against Azure Portal", version 2.1.4, enabled 2026-07-30 19:31 local. Medium, Credential Access / T1110, scheduled. TUNED, NOT SHIPPED AS-IS. This is DET-005, deliberately overlapped with the authored rule (POS-046) so one trigger tests both. TUNING 1, frequency. Shipped at "run every 1 day", which against a tenant then expiring 2026-08-13 (extended 2026-08-06 to 2026-09-14, POS-077 - the tuning decision stands on the wizard's own floor, not on the clock) means up to 24 hours per test attempt. Reduced to 1 HOUR - not the 5 minutes intended, because the wizard rejects it: with a lookback of 2 days or more the frequency must be 1 hour or greater. The lookback cannot be shortened either, since the query's own avgFailures baseline joins over ago(7d) and the wizard states query time scope is capped by rule scope. 1 hour is the floor for this rule, and the constraint is Microsoft's rather than a preference. The course material describes frequency and lookback as independent settings and does not mention the coupling, which surfaces only as a validation error after you try. TUNING 2, incident creation - and a disagreement between two surfaces. The template DETAIL PANE reads "Create incidents from this rule - Disabled". The WIZARD that instantiates it defaults the same setting to Enabled, confirmed independently by building a from-scratch rule afterwards which also defaulted Enabled. Same object, two views, opposite values, and nothing on either page indicates which is authoritative. Consequence had the pane been right: a rule producing alerts that never reach the incident queue, invisible to anyone watching incidents. WHAT A TEMPLATE ACTUALLY GIVES YOU, and it is not the query. Entity mapping arrives PRE-POPULATED - two Account entities and an IP, one Account keyed on AadUserId (a strong identifier) and one on FullName/Name/UPNSuffix (a weak composite), so the entity still resolves whichever identifier a given source supplies. That hedge is domain knowledge, not syntax. Custom details and alert details ship EMPTY, so the alert arrives with rich entities and a static title. The query is EDITABLE, confirmed by typing into it. Enabling a template forks Microsoft's KQL into a rule you own outright, which also means it will not track upstream template updates. Version 2.1.4 was pinned at enable time; whether an enabled rule ever learns about 2.1.5 is a separate and untested question. IT HAS NEVER FIRED. Presented with 7 failed sign-ins to Azure Portal on 2026-07-31, the exact activity it names, it produced nothing. It requires 10 or more failures FOLLOWED BY A SUCCESS terminating the sequence; 7 with no trailing success fails both conditions before the deviation logic is reached. Recorded as validated false, which is why the coverage matrix reads Credential Access PARTIAL (1/2) rather than COVERED. An enabled rule is a hypothesis until something proves it. One anticipated reason was eliminated by measurement: AppDisplayName logged as exactly "Azure Portal", so the scope filter matched. It failed on logic, not scope. The deviation-threshold argument was never reached and is therefore UNTESTED rather than confirmed. HALF ITS QUERY READS A TABLE THIS TENANT DOES NOT INGEST. It unions SigninLogs with AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs, a log type explicitly declined in Lab 08 (POS-034). It does not error only because union isfuzzy=true tolerates missing tables. The template runs at half coverage, silently, and nothing in the portal indicates it. Baseline before enabling: "Test with current data" returned flat zero across 50 evaluations over 7 days of real history - no false positives, and a measured starting point Lab 10 lacked.

**`POS-046` — Sentinel analytics rule - LAB-Bruteforce-Failed-Signins (authored).** LAB-Bruteforce-Failed-Signins, authored 2026-07-30 20:00 local. Scheduled, Low, Credential Access / T1110, 5-minute frequency over a 1-hour lookback, threshold above 0, group all events into a single alert, incidents enabled, alert grouping disabled. Entity mapping, custom details and alert details all built by hand. This is DET-004, the first SENTINEL detection authored in this environment. Scheduled rather than NRT, for a structural reason rather than a preference: NRT cannot aggregate over a time window, and counting failures across an hour is exactly that. NRT trades aggregation for firing on ingestion time, which makes it unsuitable for brute-force detection generally - a point the course material does not make while calling NRT the recommended default for high-priority detections. RUN 1, 2026-07-31 03:13-03:15 UTC, suppression off. Seven failed sign-ins over 92 seconds produced TWELVE ALERTS and TWELVE INCIDENTS (IDs 3-14), arriving at exactly 5-minute intervals from 03:16:11 to 04:11:11 UTC with no gaps, then stopping when the failures aged out of the lookback. THE FORMULA - alerts equals lookback divided by frequency. 60 over 5 is 12, observed exactly. Event grouping deduplicates WITHIN a run; only suppression deduplicates ACROSS runs, and the two are configured in different places. With alert grouping disabled, incidents equals alerts: twelve identical incidents, each showing one active alert, none auto-closing, all requiring individual triage for one 92-second event. This design error is recorded rather than quietly fixed: the mechanism was explained in full before the rule was built, and the rule was then built with suppression left unconfigured. Understanding a failure mode is not the same as designing against it. RUN 2, 2026-07-31 14:23-14:24 UTC, suppression ON at 1 hour. Seven failed sign-ins produced ONE alert (14:27:54 UTC, roughly 4 minutes end to end) and ONE incident (ID 15). Same rule, same trigger, one setting changed: 12 to 1 on both counts. A controlled before-and-after on a live detection. Suppression set to 1 hour deliberately, matched to the lookback - the minimum that fully deduplicates without blinding the rule to a genuinely new burst once the window clears. THE ACTIVITY SPAN - WRONG IN RUNS 1-2, THEN FIXED AND MEASURED. Runs 1 and 2 reported First and Last activity exactly 60 minutes apart, the lookback window ending at run time, for events lasting about 90 seconds - a 39x overstatement on the field an analyst reads first to judge scope. Adding "extend timestamp = StartTime", the convention Microsoft's own template carries, changed NOTHING. Replacing it with "extend TimeGenerated = StartTime" WORKS, confirmed twice: run 3 stamped 15:34:40.294 and run 4 stamped 18:19:42.226, each equal to StartTime and landing inside its own burst. The timestamp idiom is stale; TimeGenerated is the live convention. But it yields a POINT, NOT A RANGE - a summarized row has one TimeGenerated, so the alert now reports a 0-second span for a 90-second event. Neither 60 minutes nor zero is correct, and whether an alert can carry an event range from a summarized result is untested. SUPPRESSION FREEZES A MID-BURST SNAPSHOT, and this is the cost of the fix. Run 4 produced seven failures between 18:19:42 and 18:21:17; the alert reads FIVE. The rule ran after five had been ingested and before the last two, and suppression then blocked the corrected count a later run would have produced. The alert you keep is the earliest and least complete one - a 29% undercount on the number used to judge severity. Suppression trades twelve alerts for one, and the one you get under-reports the attack. Nothing in the setting indicates this. SENTINEL SCHEDULED ALERTS RECEIVE NO AUTOMATED INVESTIGATION. All thirteen incidents read Investigation state "Unsupported alert type", where Lab 10's MDO incident reads "Queued". A Sentinel-authored detection therefore produces no AIR, no investigation and no Action Center entry. This narrows Lab 03's finding that an alert is not an action: for Sentinel rules there is no action path at all, which matters before designing response around one. Incident creation lags alert generation by roughly 5 minutes, consistently across all thirteen incidents. Alert details templating WORKS, and is the clearest thing a template does not give you - alerts read "LAB-Bruteforce: 7 failed sign-ins to Azure Portal" with the FailureCount and AppDisplayName tokens resolved. Entity mapping held throughout, showing Accounts labuser on every alert in both runs. Three identifiers is the documented ceiling and the wizard enforces it by removing the Add identifier link rather than erroring. Production answer: suppression configured from the start rather than after measuring the noise, an automated response attached, and the activity-span question resolved before an analyst has to reason about scope from a field that overstates it by a factor of 39. TWO CALLS MADE DURING THIS LAB WERE WRONG AND ARE RECORDED AS SUCH. Run 3 was read as contaminated by an artifact alert that had armed suppression; it had in fact succeeded, and its alert exists at 15:34:40.294. And when run 4 reported "5 failed sign-ins to OfficeHome", the proposed explanation was that AppDisplayName splits one burst across apps below threshold. Wrong - all seven were OfficeHome, because that run used a different portal. A subsequent run at portal.azure.com logged all seven as Azure Portal, confirmed against SigninLogs. AppDisplayName is a faithful record of the entry point; the variance was in the test, not the platform.

**`POS-047` — Preset security policies (Standard, Strict).** Off is the shipped state, not a decision made here. The gap is worth recording because presets are the only configuration that stays current automatically - Microsoft updates their values as its recommendations change, where a custom policy drifts from the day it is created. The absence is stronger than the toggle suggests. Get-EOPProtectionPolicyRule and Get-ATPProtectionPolicyRule both return NOTHING - not State: Disabled, no object at all. The rule objects are created only when a preset is first enabled in the portal. So the portal renders two toggles reading off for configurations that do not exist, and PowerShell cannot distinguish "never enabled" from "does not apply" because both are silence (row 42).

**`POS-048` — Built-in protection preset (Safe Attachments and Safe Links).** THE HEADLINE FINDING OF THIS LAB. Every configuration surface reports this control healthy. Get-ATPBuiltInProtectionRule returns State: Enabled. Get-SafeAttachmentPolicy returns Action: Block, Enable: True, IsBuiltInProtection: True. The rule has a real hydration timestamp (2026-07-26, POS-036). Every scoping and exception field is empty, which in Exchange rule semantics means it applies to every recipient with no exclusions. The portal shows Status: On. Two messages were sent to the one mailbox this policy covers, two hours apart, from an external sender with clean SPF/DKIM/DMARC. NEITHER carries X-MS-Exchange-AtpMessageProperties. The two messages sent to the mailbox covered by the custom policy BOTH carry it. n=2 on each side. The portal's own note beside the toggle reads "Built-in protection is enabled only for paid Microsoft Defender for Office 365 tenants." This tenant is on trial. Whether that explains the absence is NOT established - the prediction recorded in advance was that the policy was genuinely active, and it was falsified (row 47). Nothing here is misconfigured. This is a correctly configured control, reporting healthy across four surfaces, that produced no observable effect on the traffic it claims. Configured is not effective, in its cleanest available form.

**`POS-049` — Default anti-phishing policy - impersonation protection.** The policy reads Always on and Enabled: True. Underneath, three independent layers do nothing. EnableTargetedUserProtection: False, 0 senders specified. Domain impersonation off for owned domains and 0 custom domains. Mailbox intelligence is ON and learning each mailbox's contact patterns - EnableMailboxIntelligence: True - but mailbox intelligence FOR impersonations is off, so nothing reads its output. And all three impersonation actions read "Don't apply any action", so even a detection would produce nothing. PhishThresholdLevel is 1, the least aggressive of four. All four safety tips off. The EOP half of the same policy IS live: DMARC p=quarantine quarantines, p=reject rejects, spoof intelligence moves to junk. The accurate statement is not "anti-phishing is off" - it is that EOP spoof protection works out of the box and MDO impersonation protection ships inert. Configuration analyzer independently flags 12 anti-phishing items against this policy, which is Microsoft's own measurement of the same gap. Portal detail pane and PowerShell schema agree exactly on every field checked. Recorded deliberately - surfaces disagreeing is the exception, not the rule.

**`POS-050` — Default anti-spam (inbound content filter) policy.** Four of Configuration analyzer's 18 recommendations land here, and the schema confirms each one: three actions at MoveToJmf where Standard wants Quarantine, bulk threshold 7 where Standard wants 6, and 15-day retention where Standard wants 30. HighConfidencePhishAction is already Quarantine and is the one anti-spam action the analyzer does NOT flag - two independent surfaces agreeing on both the gaps and the non-gap. The junk-versus-quarantine distinction is the substantive one. Junk mail is in the user's mailbox and one click from being opened; quarantine is not.

**`POS-051` — Default anti-malware policy.** Recorded because it is the one default in this lab that ships in a defensible state, and a register that only records failures implies failure is the norm. Zero-hour Auto Purge is on, so mail identified as malicious after delivery is retroactively removed from mailboxes. The common attachments filter is on. Quarantined malware is admin-release-only. The guide's section 6 is correct on all of these, confirmed against the schema rather than the portal. Not verified: the full FileTypes list, which the portal truncates at {ace, apk, app, appx...}.

**`POS-052` — DKIM signing for the default domain.** The portal lists a row for this domain - authoritative, default signing domain, toggle Disabled. Get-DkimSigningConfig returns NOTHING. The status value NoDKIMKeys is honest about why: there is no object, only a row rendered for a configuration that does not exist. Enabling the toggle would not change a setting, it would create one. Same shape as POS-047's preset toggles. In this portal, absence and disabled render identically (row 42). Trusted ARC sealers is likewise empty - Get-ArcConfig returns nothing. Recorded here rather than as its own entry: no third-party mail gateway exists in this environment, so the absence is correct rather than a gap.

**`POS-053` — Outbound spam filter - automatic forwarding mode.** Lab 10 authored LAB-BEC-Forwarding-Rule-Created, a DETECTIVE control for attacker-created mail forwarding, and a built-in policy fired on the same activity. Two detections for one behaviour. The PREVENTIVE control that governs whether that forwarding actually delivers mail outside the tenant had never been examined until this lab. It reads Automatic - the service decides - rather than an explicit block. Nothing is misconfigured. The finding is in the documentation: an alert was built, committed, and cross-referenced for a behaviour whose enabling setting was never recorded. Both Lab 10 alert policies are visible on the labuser entity page alongside this lab's evidence. NOT RECORDED, pending confirmation: RecipientLimitExternalPerHour and RecipientLimitInternalPerHour both read 0. In EOP, 0 conventionally denotes "use the service default" rather than "zero recipients permitted." The value reads as its own opposite and will not be transcribed until confirmed.

**`POS-054` — SA-Sales-DynamicDelivery - custom Safe Attachments policy.** The only custom threat policy in this tenant. Built and measured in Lab 12. Proven to apply by observation: both messages to the scoped mailbox carry X-MS-Exchange-AtpMessageProperties: SA, and Explorer records "Dynamic delivery-Success" on both - though only after indexing caught up. The second message read "--" at first export and carried the value on re-export of the identical query (row 50). PRECEDENCE CONFIRMED. Get-SafeAttachmentRule returns exactly this rule and does not return Built-in protection. Built-in protection's exception fields remained EMPTY after this policy was created - the service does not materialise an exclusion for sales-lab. Precedence is evaluated at mail-flow time, not written into the objects. Read both rules cold from an export and both claim every recipient (row 48). THE POLICY CARRIES A SETTING THAT CANNOT FIRE. Redirect: True with RedirectAddress populated, stored in the schema, alongside Action: DynamicDelivery. The creation wizard states in writing on the same screen that "Enable redirect only supports the Monitor action" - and then accepts the checkbox, activates the address field, validates the address format but not its applicability, renders both settings on the Review page with GREEN status dots, reports success, and persists it. Six checkpoints, one written rule, zero enforcement. No redirect copy arrived for either test message (row 43). The wizard's DEFAULT action is Off - "attachments will not be scanned by Safe Attachments" - not Block. Accepting defaults through this wizard ships a named, scoped policy that scans nothing and reads Status: On (row 44). ActionOnError is blank. The wizard never offered it. Explorer's "Dynamic delivery-Success" implies a failure state exists; that branch is undocumented and unobserved here.

**`POS-055` — Safe Attachments global settings - SharePoint/OneDrive/Teams and Safe Documents.** Recorded as inherited BY ABSENCE OF RECORD rather than as verified inheritance. Three prior sessions were searched: none configured Defender for Office 365 at all. Absent from the record is weaker than did not happen, and the audit log cannot settle it - unified audit logging was enabled 2026-07-26 at ~18:00 local, after the tenant was created. Not a hardening claim. If these were set deliberately the entry is wrong and should be corrected to hardened with a date. Operationally relevant to this lab: SharePoint/OneDrive/Teams protection being on is why the Lab 12 scope group had to be a mail-enabled security group rather than a Microsoft 365 group. An M365 group provisions a SharePoint site as a side effect, which would have introduced a second protected content surface immediately before measuring the first.

| ID | Setting | Location | State | Kind | Revisit | Verified |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `POS-056` | Email preview and download permission | `Defender > Email & collaboration > Explorer > (message) > Email entity > Email preview` | Global Administrator cannot preview or download delivered mail; quarantine only | **gap** | yes | 2026-08-01 |
| `POS-057` | Email remediation reversibility - soft delete | `Defender > Explorer > Take action > Move or delete > Soft deleted items` | Recoverable by the mailbox owner from the standard Outlook client, no notification to the operator | **gap** | yes | 2026-08-01 |

**`POS-056` — Email preview and download permission.** Observed verbatim: "You have permission to preview or download only emails that are in Quarantine. Please check permissions page or contact your admin." The identity holding total authority over this tenant cannot read the body of a delivered message. Global Administrator does not carry "Email & collaboration content (read)" - it is a separate Unified RBAC permission, deliberately gated because previewing mail is reading private correspondence. THIS SHARPENS POS-002 IN A DIRECTION THE REGISTER HAS NOT ARGUED BEFORE. Every prior entry treats the single standing Global Administrator as a RISK. This one shows it is also INSUFFICIENT: a workload exists here that the all-powerful account cannot perform. The scoped-identity argument is no longer only about least privilege; without a second role, part of the email investigation surface is simply unavailable. Not a misconfiguration. The product is correct to gate this. Recorded because the gap is invisible until an investigation needs the message body.

**`POS-057` — Email remediation reversibility - soft delete.** Measured end to end. Soft delete executed (Approval ID 6570a3, Action Center History, Approved, Completed), the message left the Inbox, and it was then restored by the mailbox owner via Deleted Items > Recover items deleted from this folder > Deletions. Two clicks, standard end-user UI, no admin involvement, no notification to the operator who remediated it. The wizard presents Junk / Deleted items / Soft deleted items / Hard deleted items as four adjacent radio buttons. The guide describes the distinction as recoverable versus permanent and frames it as operator convenience. Neither states WHO can recover. Operationally this matters most in the case remediation exists for: a BEC or phishing message in a mailbox that is compromised or whose owner is complicit. Soft-deleting it leaves the message one click from restoration by the account under investigation, and the Action Center still reads Completed. Nothing here is broken. Soft delete is documented as recoverable and that is its purpose. The gap is that the surface presenting the choice does not surface the consequence.

**`POS-059` — Pre-seeded default DLP policies.** Three of the four are ENFORCING and nobody chose any of them. Third instance of the provisioning-window pattern after Built-in protection (POS-048) and the auto-created groups - a security-relevant capability active without a decision, recorded so it is never mistaken for one. Any policy created in this tenant lands at priority 4 or below, behind all four. The Jul 14 9:39 PM stamp is now decodable as Pacific evening: the Purview policy list renders local time (Lab 14 finding).

**`POS-060` — Pre-policy classification baseline (zero change management).** Purview classifies before any policy exists - "zero change management" is Microsoft's own term for it. The three matched SITs are weakly-anchored patterns and this tenant contains only lab mail and service notifications, so these are almost certainly false positives - recorded as UNVERIFIED because verifying means opening Content explorer, which displays matched content, and the sanitization rule keeps that display-only. The value of the observation is the baseline itself: a measured false-positive floor that predates the first policy, in the same family as Built-in protection - scanning nobody enabled. Lab 14 Phase C then reproduced the mechanism deliberately: one controlled value matched two SITs at once (cross-matching).

**`POS-061` — Purview role group membership.** POS-002's Purview dimension, quantified: 70 delegation containers holding hundreds of role assignments, not one with a member. Everything Purview does in this tenant runs on Global Administrator's implicit access. Measured by CSV export (which contains no PII - group names, types, and zeroes). It pairs with POS-056 in the opposite direction: Lab 13 found GA insufficient (cannot preview delivered mail), Lab 14 found it load-bearing (the only path to any Purview capability), and the policy-creation confirmation page then showed "Permission required" on communication compliance TO Global Administrator - a third data point. The fix is harder than it reads: guide 65 records that broad Entra roles OVERRIDE scoped Purview assignments, so populating a role group produces a scoped identity only if that identity holds no overriding Entra role. Closes only when a scoped analyst identity does real work (POS-002's standing condition). AMENDED 2026-08-03: first deliberate membership - the admin account was added to the Insider Risk Management role group (the full 17-role group; narrower groups rejected for lab purposes) at 07:50 PDT to enable Lab 15's alert surfaces. This is a capability grant to the SAME identity, not POS-002's scoped analyst - the gap this entry records narrows by one group and does not close. Propagation measured: the IRM Policies page banner ("you aren't assigned to a role group that allows you to view alerts") still rendered past the documented one-hour ceiling while the Alerts grid itself served content by ~09:00 - the warning outlived the condition it warned about. The GA-insufficiency family this entry anchors reached five measured instances across three solutions: mail preview (POS-056), communication compliance, DLP sensitive-info details (Data Classification Content Viewer), IRM alert viewing (this grant's cause) - against Adaptive Protection rendering fully to GA unaided.

**`POS-062` — Lab DLP policy - US Financial, simulation mode, template defaults.** Deliberately all-defaults so the defaults themselves are the measurement. What defaults ship: seven locations blanket-enabled (two non-functional here, and those same two unsupported by simulation mode); notify-and-report on (tips, threshold 10, incident reports, alerts) with the only enforcement action OFF; the entire device-action section off, so Devices is in scope and uninstrumented; 15-day auto-enable unchecked (verified - it would have fired 2026-08-17, which at the time was past the trial's 2026-08-13 death). Incident reports cover four of the seven in-scope locations. AMENDED 2026-08-06 - THIS PARENTHETICAL IS NOW FALSE AND THE CONCLUSION SURVIVES ON DIFFERENT GROUNDS. The trial was extended to 2026-09-14 (POS-077), so 2026-08-17 now falls INSIDE the tenant's life rather than past its end. The 15-day auto-enable timer is no longer foreclosed by expiry. Nothing changes operationally - the checkbox ships unchecked and was verified unchecked, so no timer is running - but the reason the override was "not needed" was partly that the tenant would be dead first, and that reason is void. If the policy is ever moved off simulation mode, the auto-enable state must be re-read rather than assumed harmless. PHASE D OUTCOME (2026-08-03): EFFECTIVE for the covered paths, measured. Detected the pre-validated content at rest (OneDrive, including content predating activation) and in transit (Exchange, evaluated at the send minute, twice), with exact per-SIT attribution (ABA 1 Medium / Bank Account 2 Medium, Low volume rule). Report indexing lags evaluation by 8-12 minutes. Restart-the-simulation is a destructive rebuild that wipes unrecoverable real-time history behind a consequence-free confirmation dialog - the policy detects; its evidence surface is fragile. Devices produced nothing through three stacked mechanisms (no at-rest device scan, device actions off, endpoints deallocated), as predicted.

**`POS-063` — Insider Risk Management org-level indicators - Microsoft's pre-selected recommended set accepted verbatim.** Two findings, one entry. First, the baseline: IRM ships with EVERY indicator off - the inverse of DLP's posture two labs earlier, where seven locations arrived blanket-enabled and scoped All (POS-062). Two Purview solutions, provisioned in the same window, shipping opposite defaults. DLP defaults to watching everything and enforcing nothing; IRM defaults to watching nothing at all. Second, the enablement is not a decision the operator gets to skip. The policy wizard forces the dialog and pre-selects Microsoft's recommended set; accepting it is one click and declining it leaves the policy unable to score. What was accepted is therefore a vendor judgment, not ours - recorded here as such rather than as a hardening choice. Three surfaces disagree on how many indicators exist. The chooser renders 17 categories; the policy screen renders 12 categories with different per-category totals; the review page states "45/126". No two agree, and the 103 figure used above is this repository's count from the chooser. The disagreement is the durable fact. Timestamp debt recorded honestly: the save minute was never captured at the time and is reconstructed only as "~08:45 PDT" from surrounding wall-clock anchors (role group 07:50, policy creation 08:52).

**`POS-064` — Lab IRM policy - Data leaks template, DLP-match trigger against a simulation-mode policy.** Built to answer one question: does a SIMULATION-MODE DLP match function as an IRM triggering event? Answer, measured over 49 hours across three independent surfaces: NO - and nothing anywhere says so. The trigger dropdown listed all five tenant DLP policies with ZERO mode or severity annotation, while the same wizard screen states the DLP policy "must be configured to generate 'High' severity incident reports". The selector does not enforce the requirement the wizard states one paragraph away. OUTCOME (2026-08-05): NULL, confirmed twice on each surface. Trigger email sent 09:11 PDT 2026-08-03 and MATCHED - Lab 14's report carries it as LAB15 TRIGGER TEST.eml, Exchange, Aug 3 4:11 PM UTC, Low volume rule, U.S. Bank Account +1 more. So the triggering event's precondition demonstrably occurred. At +25 h and again at +49 h: Alerts (preview) 0 items, no first-alert notification email in either inbox tab, Active alerts 0, Last alert "No alerts yet". ONE null, FOUR candidate causes - not four independent rejections. They are not co-equal: (c) Users in scope = 0, persistent across 49 h, would PREEMPT the others, since a policy with no scored population may never have evaluated the trigger at all, leaving (a) simulation-mode and (b) the unenforced High-severity requirement no opportunity to reject anything. (d) non-evaluation upstream is indistinguishable from (c). And (c) is itself uncertain: the grid reads 0 while the flyout on the same screen reports coverage of all active users at High (divergence row 83). Two surfaces, one field, no third surface to break the tie. The leading candidate rests on believing the persistent reading on the field named for the question - recorded as a choice, not as a measurement. Mechanism open. Status read Healthy at creation and "1 warning" from 2026-08-04 onward with no configuration change between. The warning is "Physical badging data isn't being uploaded" - an unconfigured optional connector, irrelevant to a DLP-triggered policy. The health job is demonstrably live (last-updated stamp moved 08-04 09:08 -> 08-05 04:38) and has reported that same irrelevant warning on every pass while saying nothing about zero users in scope or a trigger that cannot fire. Policy alert effectiveness renders 0% - a computed metric over an empty set, presented as a definite number. Recorded omission: Microsoft's own checklist marks "Configure insider risk settings" REQUIRED and it was skipped. Defaults-as-shipped everywhere except the org indicator toggle (POS-063).

**`POS-065` — Entra directory role Purview Workload Content Reader, auto-assigned to the standing GA identity outside PIM.** SECOND cross-product side-effect provisioning measured in this repository, and structurally identical to the first. Two minutes after the admin was added to the Insider Risk Management role group at 07:50 PDT (POS-061), a Microsoft-operated principal assigned an ENTRA DIRECTORY role - a different permission system entirely. Causation is inference from two-minute proximity and is labelled as such; the assigner name (PurviewRoleAssignmentMigrator) supports it. The sibling case: Lab 14's DLP policy creation caused MIP to auto-create two mirror file policies and auto-enable file monitoring in MDCA (Lab 16). One action in one product silently provisioning state in another is now a pattern, not an anomaly. Note what it did NOT grant. Purview still reports that "Data Classification Content Viewer" is required to view sensitive info details (divergence row 80). An automated process granted a content-reader role that is not the content-reader role the UI demands - two similarly named roles, neither implying the other. Open question rather than a claim. This entry is kind: weakening because the tenant's privileged surface grew without a decision. It narrows nothing about POS-002, which stays open.

**`POS-066` — MDCA policy census at provisioning - 23 of 26 built-in policies disabled by platform migration.** The June 15 2025 dynamic threat detection model migration disabled the anomaly-policy objects; the page carries the banner. Guide 53's claim that a substantial set ships enabled is STALE - the largest accumulator correction of the course arc so far. The migration took UEBA and left threat intelligence: the three survivors are all OAuth/TI policies, not behavioural ones. Labelled as inference from the survivor set, not from documentation. The policy list is therefore NOT a detection inventory. 23 objects that look like configured detections are inert placeholders for a model that runs somewhere this page does not show. Same family as the Sentinel three-surface detection count (divergence row 41): asking "what is running" of a list that answers "what exists".

**`POS-067` — MDCA file monitoring and two mirror file policies - auto-provisioned by a DLP policy created in a different product.** FIRST cross-product side-effect provisioning measured in this repository (POS-065 is the second). Lab 14's DLP policy creation caused Microsoft Information Protection to create two CAS file policies - one per compiled DLP rule - AND to flip the file-monitoring toggle, in a product that had not been opened. The MDCA Activity log holds only five events total and every one of them is this. CORRECTION RECORDED: an earlier claim in this repository that file monitoring had been ON "since provisioning" was WRONG. The Activity log proved our own Lab 14 action flipped it. Corrected in-session rather than carried. WITHDRAWAL RECORDED: the 17:52 mirror-creation timestamp was read as approximately corresponding to DLP sync completion. That inference is withdrawn - the DLP simulation-completion alert email self-stamps 16:06 local (2026-08-02 11:06 PM UTC), leaving a 1 h 46 m gap the inference cannot cover. Mechanism reopened and unexplained. The mirrors reading 0 while their source reads 2 is the sharper half: objects that exist, list as ACTIVE, carry severities and an alert bell, and register nothing the policy that spawned them registers. Configured is not effective, in the most literal available form.

**`POS-068` — Microsoft 365 app connector - Connected, and silent.** THREE independent surfaces agree the connector carries no user telemetry: the Activity log holds five events, all administrative; the CloudAppEvents table in advanced hunting returns 0 rows over 7 days; the connector's own Last activity column reads a dash. Three-surface agreement is why this is recorded as genuine no-flow rather than as a rendering problem. Leading suspect ELIMINATED: unified audit is ON (System > Audit renders the full search interface). The obvious cause is ruled out and no replacement has been found. Recorded as unexplained-with-obvious-cause- eliminated rather than left implicitly attributed. "Connected" therefore joins the status-label family alongside Healthy (POS-064), Available, and Completed. It describes a configuration relationship, not a data flow, and nothing on the page distinguishes them. This entry is the strongest available explanation for POS-069's zero, and the reason that zero is recorded as divergence-with-mechanism-open rather than as a calibration result. MECHANISM RESOLVED 2026-08-12, eight days later, and it was a configuration this entry had no reason to suspect. The connector's own Select Microsoft 365 components page carries six checkboxes. FIVE ARE UNCHECKED - Microsoft Entra ID Management events, Microsoft Entra ID Sign-in events, Microsoft Entra ID Apps, MICROSOFT 365 ACTIVITIES, and Microsoft 365 files. The sixth, Microsoft Entra Users and groups, is checked and greyed - it cannot be unchecked. That single enabled component is what Protected accounts 3 reports on, and it is the whole of what this connector collects. Microsoft's own advanced hunting documentation names this exact control as the prerequisite: "To make sure the CloudAppEvents table is populated: Go to the Defender portal and select Settings > Cloud apps > App connectors. In the Select Microsoft 365 components page, select the Microsoft 365 activities checkbox." (advanced-hunting-cloudappevents-table, ms.date 05/15/2025.) The page itself states the consequence: "unchecked options prevent some security features from functioning properly." So the answer was documented and on-screen the entire time, three non-obvious interactions away from every surface that reports health. The route: select the row's CHECKBOX to reveal an action bar above the table, then Edit settings. The overflow menu item literally labelled "View App connector settings" navigates to a filtered list view, not to settings. Cancel on the components wizard drops the connector context entirely. TEST CONNECTION: SUCCESS IS NOT EVIDENCE OF EFFECTIVE COLLECTION. Run live on 2026-08-12, the connector's Test connection returned Success in green, and Last health check read "an hour ago" on two readings roughly an hour apart - so a scheduled check is running and passing. It was passing against a connector with Microsoft 365 activities unchecked, five of six components disabled, and the expected activity absent. The test establishes that authentication and reachability work. It establishes nothing about whether anything is being collected. This is recorded here as supporting evidence for the resolved mechanism rather than as a separate divergence row: it is one evidence chain, not an independent expected-versus-observed claim. Connected / Healthy / Success are not effective telemetry collection. CORROBORATION EXTENDED. CloudAppEvents now reads 0 rows ACROSS ALL TIME, not 0 over 7 days - a bare | count, with AlertInfo (30 rows) and DeviceLogonEvents (86) in the same session as the control proving the query surface works. The connector's own app dashboard renders Active users and Activity chart both flat at zero across 07/12 to 08/11 with a blank location map. Five surfaces now, spanning a month. DELIBERATELY NOT REMEDIATED. The checkbox is left unchecked. Turning it on is a configuration change that earns its own predeclared measurement list - first-arrival latency into CloudAppEvents, whether it backfills, when Last activity moves, how long the dashboard charts take - rather than being flipped as a side effect of an investigation. The default as provisioned is now recorded, which is what makes that experiment possible later. revisit stays true: the mechanism is closed, the remediation decision is open.

**`POS-069` — Lab MDCA file policy - DCS inspection against the Lab 14 SITs, advanced settings untouched.** Built as a cross-product calibration experiment. Advanced settings were deliberately untouched so that defaults-as-shipped IS the measurement: Purview's DCS and MDCA's DCS, same engine family, same three SITs, same file. OUTCOME: Purview matched the file at Medium confidence (U.S. Bank Account 2 Medium / 2 Low, ABA Routing 1 Medium / 1 Low, High confidence absent on both) and surfaced it within minutes. MDCA read 0 at +3 h 30 m and again at +27 h. Two-read rule satisfied; MDCA file scans carry no published SLA, so a zero is a claim about the scan or the index, not about the file. The zero CANNOT be resolved into "scanned and below threshold" versus "never scanned", and POS-068 makes the second live. Recorded as DIVERGENCE WITH MECHANISM OPEN, not as a calibration verdict. The operator-facing fact stands regardless: content Purview flags at Medium is invisible to an MDCA default file policy at 27 hours. Defaults worth recording from the build: the wizard pre-seeds Access level = Public/External plus a last-modified cutoff, so the DEFAULT SCOPE EXCLUDES PRIVATE FILES - a default-accepting operator builds a policy blind to internal-only content. Both were removed here. "Inspect protected files" is greyed pending an Entra permission grant to the MDCA application (application-consent, not GA-insufficiency). The SIT picker offers 325 where Purview twice reported 327.

**`POS-070` — MDCA to Defender for Endpoint integration - enforcement off, alerting pre-armed.** The reverse of the enabled-but-inert pattern this repository usually records: here the ENFORCEMENT is off and the ALERTING for it is on. A notification is pre-armed for an event the configuration makes impossible. Completes an asymmetry taxonomy visible across the whole MDCA surface - data-plane visibility ON by default (the connector, POS-068), endpoint and third-party integration OFF by default, enforcement OFF by default. The defaults are consistently permissive about seeing and consistently conservative about acting, which is defensible; the alert toggle is the one element that does not fit either half. Open: the MDE-side discovery toggle was never read, so only one direction of this integration is measured.

**`POS-071` — Incident 1 triage state.** Module 77's trap sprung and sidestepped: all three alerts traced to lab-controlled activity (MDE onboarding validation script twice; Azure Run Command delivering the onboarding package itself), so True positive and False positive were both wrong. The detections were accurate; the activity was ours. Resolving the incident zeroed its member alerts (Related alerts 2/3 to 0/3) - incident-to-alert propagation observed downward, having earlier been observed absent upward (AIR resolving an alert never touched the incident header).

**`POS-072` — Microsoft Sentinel Responder for the analyst identity.** Scope was a recorded decision: RG rather than workspace, because Sentinel is a resource family - playbooks (Logic Apps), workbooks, and automation artifacts live beside the workspace, and G57's Playbook Operator grant composes at the same layer. The trade-off is stated, not hidden: least privilege argues workspace scope; against non-Sentinel resources in the group the role's Sentinel-shaped actions grant almost nothing useful, and the practical delta is workspace read/query visibility on any LAW in the group plus automatic inheritance by future resources - convenience and risk being the same property. A workspace-scoped attempt was caught by reading the breadcrumb and backed out; the two wizards differ (the RG wizard carries an Assignment type tab the workspace wizard lacks), and that tab silently produced Eligible time-bound where the plan assumed Active permanent. The IAM Role assignments grid, not the wizard summary, is the state surface. Eligibility does not close POS-002 - the Global Administrator still does the work - but the mechanism its production column has named since Lab 00 now exists and runs here.

The observation worth keeping: the privilege-elevation path enforced stronger authentication than the tenant baseline does. Nothing tenant-wide requires MFA here; activating a PIM role did. PIM compensated, per-elevation, for controls the tenant never deployed.

**`POS-074` — Incident 19 triage state (the Responder boundary test artifact).** A deliberate, attributed state change: both writes were made as analyst under an activated Sentinel Responder role and are the lab's evidence that the role performs its documented function on both surfaces. The unified portal refused the same write at T+17 min post-activation with "You're missing permissions to manage this incident" - a claim about the identity that was only true of the cache; see the divergence table.

**`POS-075` — Two Sentinel automation rules, both Standard, ordered.** The two rules were built from the two different entry points on purpose, to observe the constraint models: the Automation-page builder arrives empty and free (the value picker enumerated three analytic rules - including Fusion / Advanced Multistage Attack Detection, which the Analytics management list does not show - and let you choose), while the analytics-rule path arrives with the condition pre-populated and LOCKED to a late-bound Current rule token, operator and value both greyed. Same feature, two surfaces, two binding semantics: enumerated-at-creation vs resolved-at-runtime (rename-safe). Both rules are Standard; the Automation page's Create path and the analytics-rule path both produce Standard, while the Enhanced kind (alert-trigger only, tenant-wide) is a separate engine the source guide never mentions.

**`POS-076` — Both automation rules fire on one incident, in order, ~11 s after creation.** Retroactivity (P79-2) confirmed by diff: the 22 pre-existing incidents were byte-identical after the rules fired, save incident 19's Lab-17 In-Progress write already in the baseline. Nothing retroactive - the rules touched only the incident created after they existed, as Microsoft claims. The audit log surfaced an anomaly invisible everywhere else: at 18:12:27.986Z - 3 ms after its assignment - Rule B logged a second Tags changed to auto-tagged-ruleA under its own identity, though its only action is Assign owner. The likeliest mechanism is that a second-in-order rule re-commits the incident's full managed-state post-image (which by then includes Rule A's tag) and the audit records the write under B. The tag is idempotent so the outcome is correct and the queue, header, and chip all read clean; the duplicate exists only at millisecond resolution in the audit log. Outcome correct, record shows work that did not happen, visible only where no one looks - the repository's recurring shape, now inside its own automation.

**`POS-081` — Playbook managed identity — Entra directory role.** Granted so the playbook's PATCH to /users/{upn} would succeed. Directory scope and permanent activation were both accepted for lab convenience; neither is defensible in production for an identity that can reset any user's password unattended. THE GRANT BOUGHT MORE THAN IT WAS MADE FOR, and that is the finding. Two actions after the reset, HTTP - get manager reads /users/{upn}/manager on the same managed identity. Nobody granted directory read with that call in mind. It returned 200 (verified 2026-08-08, run 11:57:47 PDT). WHY IT MATTERS. Had the role been narrower, that read would have failed, the run would still have reported Succeeded, and the template's else branch would have written the plaintext temporary password into the Sentinel incident comment - readable by any Sentinel Reader and persisting beyond run history's retention. Over-permission is what kept the credential out of the incident. Narrowing this role without first reading the workflow definition would create a credential disclosure. See divergence row 144 and labs/19 section 7. PIM MECHANICS OBSERVED: the member picker will not browse service principals - the object ID is required - and the picker's own tab list is a function of the result set (an Enterprise applications tab did not exist until a GUID search returned one). Permanently assigned ships checked while the greyed Assignment ends field shows a date ~180 days out; the checkbox governs.

**`POS-082` — Sentinel service principal — Azure RBAC on the playbook resource group.** Required for Sentinel to launch a playbook. Withheld deliberately on the first attempt to isolate causation, which produced the lab's headline finding: Sentinel validates this permission at RULE-CREATION time, not at run time. Without it the automation rule will not create at all - ARM BadRequest, "Missing required permissions for Microsoft Sentinel on the playbook resource". The identical form resubmitted after the grant succeeded (divergence row 136). SCOPE IS BROADER THAN THE NEED. Granted at resource-group scope because that is what the guide and the portal path make easy. Any playbook later created in rg-soc-lab is launchable by Sentinel without a further decision. Recorded as hardened because the control is correctly in place and the alternative is a non-functioning automation rule; the scope is the part to revisit. THREE identically-named `Azure Security Insights` applications appear in the picker. Identification is by object ID, not by name.

**`POS-083` — Playbook mail connection — delegated OAuth as the tenant owner.** Observed at runtime 2026-08-08: the security notification arrived From Lab Administrator To Lab Administrator - the recipient is also the apparent sender. A copy lands in the sending mailbox's Sent Items, doubling the plaintext credential's mail footprint (see POS-084). NOT A CHOICE IN THE TEMPLATE. The Office 365 Outlook connector offers no managed-identity option, so the identity model is inherited from the connector rather than selected. The two Graph calls in the same workflow use the managed identity; only the mail action is delegated. One run, two principals. CONSEQUENCES. Automated security mail is indistinguishable from mail the recipient sent; it passes SPF/DKIM/DMARC as a legitimate internal send, so no anti-spoofing control will ever flag it; and the audit trail attributes an automated action to a human. Microsoft ships the message at Low importance.

**`POS-084` — Logic Apps run-history data protection — secure inputs and outputs.** Verified at runtime: the temporary password rendered in PLAINTEXT in run history on HTTP - reset a password Inputs, and again in the mail action's Inputs. Default run-history retention is 90 days. The workflow type is Stateful, which is what causes every action's inputs and outputs to be persisted at all - two settings at default jointly producing the exposure, neither of them a decision anyone made. OFF IS ABSENT, NOT FALSE. There is no runtimeConfiguration.secureData property on the action. The designer renders toggles for a property that does not exist until it is set. Nobody disabled the protection; nobody enabled it. THE CREDENTIAL IS NOT THE ONLY SECRET LOGGED. HTTP - get manager carries no $select, so Graph returned the full user object - displayName, mail, userPrincipalName, and the account holder's business phone number - all persisted for the same 90 days to satisfy a workflow that reads one field. ROTATION DOES NOT CLEAN THE LOG. The credential was rotated 2026-08-08 (labs/19 section 5). The run-history and mailbox copies remain until retention expires or they are deleted. Recorded so the rotation is not mistaken for remediation of the exposure. GENERATOR WEAKNESS, recorded but not the headline: the template builds the password as substring(guid(), 0, 10) - nine lowercase-hex characters plus a hyphen, ~36 bits, single-case alphabet. An all-numeric draw (~1.5%) or an all-alpha draw (~0.014%) yields two character classes and should fail Entra complexity. Predicted, not observed; n=1 and the sample was mixed.

**`POS-085` — Authentication methods — registration campaign.** Found by elimination after a password change unexpectedly demanded MFA registration. Security Defaults are Disabled (POS-001) and the Conditional Access policy list is EMPTY - the blade rendered its What is Conditional Access / Get Started empty state, and all 28 rows in the 24-hour sign-in log read Conditional Access: Not Applied. SO NOTHING IN THE TENANT REQUIRED IT, AND IT HAPPENED ANYWAY. This inverts the repository's recurring shape. The usual finding is configured-and-ineffective; this is unconfigured-and-in-force. The tenant cannot answer "is a registration campaign enabled here" from its own configuration, because Microsoft holds the state and the blade says so: settings may be updated over time without administrator action. OBSERVED EFFECT: five separate 50072 interrupts (user must enroll in MFA) between 12:29 and 12:39 PDT on 2026-08-08, each followed by a successful single-factor sign-in - snooze behaviour, consistent with the greyed `Days allowed to snooze: 1`. ONE DISCREPANCY, UNRESOLVED. The blade states the campaign's method is Passkey (FIDO2); the sign-in screens offered Microsoft Authenticator. Either the tenant surfaces a different method when a passkey nudge cannot proceed, or something other than the campaign produced the interrupt. Not established. Microsoft may also have changed the setting between the event and the read.

**`POS-086` — `labuser` — MFA registration outstanding, account left in service.** EXPLICIT DECISION, recorded rather than left implicit. The MFA registration prompted during Lab 19's remediation was not completed, and no replacement identity was created. WHY IT IS SAFE FOR THE LAB'S PURPOSE. The interrupt fires only on SUCCESSFUL interactive sign-in. labuser's entire role is generating 50126 failures for DET-004, which never authenticate and never reach the interrupt. Verified against the 2026-08-08 sign-in log: the seven-failure volley produced no interrupt; the interrupts appeared only after a successful sign-in during remediation. THE STATED REASON HAS ALREADY EXPIRED, and this is why the entry is worded this way. The original reason for not creating a replacement was the 25-to-1 licence cliff on 2026-08-14. That will pass. The decision remains correct on different grounds: labuser carries First Seen 2026-07-17 and eleven labs of telemetry continuity, and a fresh identity would fork that for no gain. Same shape as POS-058 - a decision whose reason expired while the decision stayed correct is exactly the kind a future reader inherits wrongly. WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT. Any future lab requiring a successful interactive sign-in as labuser will meet the interrupt. Handle it then, deliberately, with the before and after recorded - not by completing registration mid-session, which would alter the tenant's failed-signin telemetry generator without a baseline.

**`POS-087` — Security Copilot capacity - 1 provisioned SCU, overage limited to 0.** The resource exists no longer; the entry records the configuration and the two things measured through it. OVERAGE HAS NO OFF. The Enable Overage Capacity toggle will not disable. The ARM template confirms why - the schema carries overageState and overageAmount, and there is no Disabled value. Zero is expressed as state Limited with amount 0. The form default is Allow Unlimited Overage Capacity, so the as-shipped configuration has no upper bound. DEMAND EXCEEDED CAPACITY AND WAS ABSORBED. Three prompts consumed 1.5 units against 1 provisioned. Overage read 0 of 0 throughout. The at-capacity tooltip states Microsoft does not charge for the extra units needed to finish an in-flight operation. This appears in none of the course guides. An earlier claim that the unlimited default would have billed 6 USD for that 0.5 is WITHDRAWN - the evidence does not support it, and what the cap prevented on this session is unknown. The decision to bound overage stands on its own reasoning under a fixed ceiling. P20-11 IS OPEN. The 4 USD figure is inferred from the billing model and the 11:00-12:00 clock-hour window. Cost analysis reported nothing on the day. Given POS-016 was forced by a 43 percent gap between tracked and actual spend, the amount is not asserted until an invoice confirms it.

**`POS-088` — Security Copilot ownership granted to seven Entra directory roles by default.** Owner rights cover usage monitoring, owner settings, plugin management and role assignment. The grant is to ROLES, not to named principals, so any future holder of Intune Administrator inherits Copilot ownership with no action taken and no notification. THIS QUALIFIES MOD-82. The committed claim is that Copilot inherits the analyst's permissions and cannot reach past a boundary the user could not cross. That holds for DATA. It does not hold for CONTROL: ownership of the Copilot service is Copilot-native, assigned at setup, and was assigned to seven directory roles by default. Two permission models on one product, and the guide describes one. Contributors were changed from the default. The wizard pre-selected Select from recommended Microsoft Security contributor roles with a Microsoft Entra roles group already ticked. Set to No one - add them later, because only admin uses this tenant and an unused access grant is still an access grant in a repo that documents every one.

**`POS-089` — Security Copilot data-sharing and audit-logging defaults at first run.** The payload matters here. Prompts in this tenant carry labuser's UPN, the tenant domain, and the lab public IPv4 - three .pii-terms entries - plus an Entra object ID and a User SID that are not in the wordlist. Shipped defaults would have routed that to human review. THE MODEL-TRAINING TOGGLE QUALIFIES MOD-82's assurance that customer data is not used to train foundation models. Not necessarily a contradiction - a security AI model may be a different object from a foundation model, and the control is opt-out rather than silent - but a flat assurance does not survive a screen that ships both switches on. PURVIEW LOGGING OFF IS NOT FREE. Off means prompt and response content does not reach Purview's audit store, so these sessions leave no Purview record. Same shape as POS-084 inverted: there the control was absent and a credential persisted; here the control is present, set safe, and the evidence trail thins. Both are real; neither is costless. ONE DEFAULT RAN THE CUSTOMER'S WAY. Purview access to Customer Data shipped off. Recorded because the easy generalisation - that every default favours Microsoft's access - is falsified inside its own lab. The accurate statement is narrower: the defaults that ship ON govern Microsoft's own collection.
